articles.title: How Candle House’s Immersive Theater Show ‘The Pineapple’ Became a Spooky L.A. Hit, Playing 76 Shows With Just One Ticket for Each Performance
articles.summary: Part of the thrill of theater is that you’re taking part in a one-time experience, never to be recorded or repeated, in which anyone who wasn’t part of that live audience with you will simply have to take your word for how it was. Still, you may seek out clues about whether your experience of
body: But what if there were no other audience members? (As in, deliberately… not because it was a night of badly promoted equity-waiver theater.) No friends or strangers to share immediate laughs or gasps with, let alone notes afterward? Just a small cast of actors and you, paying for the privilege of being an audience of one?

Add to this the idea that the play — about which you’re meant to know little in advance, beyond the fact that it may involve supernatural elements — takes place in a secret location, revealed only at the last minute, and even then not through anything so obvious as an actual street address. For anyone with a shy bone in their bodies, it can sound a little intimidating, knowing a band of actors is going to collectively train its sole attention on you, even before getting to the scariest aspect of all: There will be audience participation. That means you, bub.

articles.title: ‘The First Taste of Loneliness’ Review: A Sentimental but Affecting Study of Family Life After Bereavement
articles.summary: The most moving scene in “The First Taste of Loneliness” is not, in fact, its most tear-streaked. Gu You’s heartfelt family portrait opens on an extended, anguished scene of three women — a mother, her daughter and her granddaughter — keeping vigil at the bedside of their beloved husband, father…
body: Chinese director Gu You's conclusion to his 'Landscape' trilogy too often steps into maudlin territory, but rights itself whenever it focuses on everyday details in its portrait of three generations of grieving women.

Somewhat heavily expository dialogue informs us that Yue, formerly a fashion director in Beijing, has recently returned with Moon to the family apartment in the city of Hangzhou in southeast China. Home to Luna and her late husband for decades, it’s a roomy, rambling space with spectacular views of the Qiantang River and, in Zhou Xingyu’s excellent production design, a storied buildup of clutter. Mikiya Takimoto’s camera lingers affectionately on stacked bookshelves — not even old cassette tapes have been thrown away — and desktops heavy with ornaments, notes and photographs that reveal in shorthand a life rich in love. Even in death, the man maintains a palpable presence in the home.

articles.title: Philippines Revamps International Co-Production Fund With Minority and Majority Tracks, Unveiled at Busan Market
articles.summary: The Philippines has revamped its International Co-Production Fund (ICOF) around two tracks, with the amount of cash on offer tied to the size of the Filipino stake in a project.
body: The Film Philippines Office (FPO) unveiled the new framework at the Busan International Film Festival ‘s Asian Contents & Film Market.

The Minority Track is for international productions in which a Filipino producer is the junior partner. Features and series can draw up to PHP7 million ($113,000), with documentaries and shorts capped at PHP3 million ($48,000).

The bar is lower here. Filipino producers need a stake of 10% or more, and the production must hire either two Filipino above-the-line talents or three Filipino crew members in key creative or technical roles. Applicants must also show how the film will reach audiences outside the Philippines.

Both tracks offer the same top-ups. Qualifying ASEAN co-productions earn an extra PHP1 million ($16,000), and projects that clear a cultural test can collect up to PHP2 million ($32,000) more. The FPO noted that the dollar figures may vary with exchange rates.

articles.title: ‘Blade Runner 2099’ Drops New Trailer, Team Teases a Detective Story Set When Replicants Take Over
articles.summary: The limited series cast, showrunner and EPs discussed how the lives of Michelle Yeoh’s dying Replicant and Hunter Schafer's undercover human will intertwine at NYCC on Saturday.
body: Prime Video released a new Blade Runner 2099 trailer during the upcoming series’ New York Comic Con panel on Saturday.

Michelle Yeoh, Hunter Schafer, Dimitri Abold, Lewis Gribben, Matthew Needham, showrunner Silka Luisa, and executive producers Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson appeared on the Saturday evening panel, where the cast and creative team teased what’s in store for fans of the franchise and how the series will be different than its film installments.

Speaking to her human character, Schafer shared she is “more or less a fugitive in hiding from LAPD Blade Runners. Her work gets raided, and she’s gotta go on the run and make sure she protects her little brother, and ultimately undergo this mission where she goes undercover as a Blade Runner with LAPD.” Yeoh teased that her character is dying in the limited series: “She knows the time is running out, and she’s a character that doesn’t like to leave things unfinished.”

During a clip shown exclusively to the room, Yeoh’s character can be seen with blue-like nail beds, which Luisa explained was inspired by the original Blade Runner film and indicates Yeoh’s character is dying.

articles.title: ‘I just wasn’t going to give up’: the fight to free the longest-serving political prisoner in the US
articles.summary: Leonard Peltier was imprisoned for 49 years before his sentence was commuted. A new Netflix documentary exposes the ‘corrupt’ system that allowed it to happen. On 20 January 2025, with 14 minutes remaining in his term as president, Joe Biden commuted the life sentence of Leonard Peltier, after…
body: Outside the Florida prison where Peltier was being held that morning were several of the many activists and lawyers who fought for his release, as well as film-makers David France and Jesse Short Bull. The two directors’ long-gestating documentary on Peltier’s fight for justice was set to premiere just a week later at the Sundance film festival with a very different ending, the octogenarian still awaiting a chance to return home to the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa reservation in North Dakota. That morning, there was “a sinking feeling that it wasn’t going to happen”, France said.

When it did, while the cameras rolled, the line of supporters erupted in joy for a commutation that allowed Peltier to serve the rest of his consecutive life sentences on house arrest, though it did not pardon him – not quite justice, but a victory so uncertain and so hard-fought, over more than half a lifetime, that I have cried every time I’ve rewatched it.

articles.title: Roy Scheider Was In A Forgettable Sequel To A Genre-Defining Sci-Fi Movie
articles.summary: Did you know Stanley Kubrick's landmark sci-fi film 2001: A Space Odyssey got a sequel (starring Roy Scheider, no less)? Here's why it's mostly been forgotten.
body: Yes, "2001: A Space Odyssey" received a sequel. Titled "2010: The Year We Make Contact," it stars Roy Scheider and even scored five Oscar nods. It's also been more or less forgotten these days.

"2001: A Space Odyssey" was co-written by Arthur C. Clarke, who published the novel version of "2001" a few months after the release of Kubrick's movie. He went on to write several books and short stories in the 1970s (including "Rendezvous with Rama" in 1973) before returning to the world of "2001" with "2010: Odyssey Two" in 1982. Sci-fi fans rejoiced, and Hollywood licked its lips.

In 1984, writer/director Peter Hyams released a big-budget feature film adaptation of "Odyssey Two" titled, you guessed it, "2010: The Year We Make Contact." However, the movie was a bit of a financial disappointment, which may have discouraged studios from adapting Clarke's other two "2001" sequel novels ("2061: Odyssey Three" and "3001: The Final Odyssey"). It didn't help that "2010" lacks the awe, mystery, and psychedelic nature of Kubrick's "2001," focusing more on plot and practical matters. Its visual effects are cool, though.

articles.title: Ray Gunn review – Brad Bird’s animated film-noir sci-fi caper is an old-school family classic
articles.summary: Sam Rockwell voices the gumshoe who becomes embroiled with Scarlett Johansson’s femme fatale in this big-hearted and beautifully designed fantasy spectacular. Brad Bird, the Spielberg of animation, applies his masterly authorial touch to a terrific family film that retrieves the genre from the…
body: When Venus discovers his planned scam, she threatens to kill Arnold in front of witnesses, creating a murderous cloud over her reputation – but malevolent Arnold has something on her too. It all leads to a scary plot, involving Venus’s smoothie manager and first husband Barry (Alan Tudyk) and fez-wearing nightclub proprietor and mob boss Slugsy (Matt Berry), who comes on like a cross between Sydney Greenstreet and Jabba the Hutt.

There are some lovely set piece scenes – especially when Ray and Venus take to the floor at a club which offers a “zero gravity” interlude allowing its dancers and lovers the chance to float surreally around as if in space. We also get a bizarre interlude when a gun turns out to be – temporarily – capable of scrambling the limbs of those in its sights. And on top of all that, the film has something to say about algorithmic ads and data privacy. It’s a charming, very enjoyable movie with a big heart.

articles.title: Joseph Gordon-Levitt Says Instead of Being Afraid of AI, “We Should Be Concerned About the People Building AI”
articles.summary: "These models are being trained to hijack your intimacy, to make friends with you, to get you to fall in love with it," the actor said of technology's training.
body: Joseph Gordon-Levitt, who was appointed the United Nations’ first global advocate for human-centric digital governance in March, is arguing that instead of being afraid of AI, “we should be concerned about the people building AI.”

In a new video interview with The New York Times, the actor was asked his current biggest fear about the technology. “I would object to that question just because reducing these concerns into one sound bite of fear — that’s one of the problems,” Gordon-Levitt responded.

The Don Jon star previously opened up about his concerns about AI, arguing at a panel hosted by The Hollywood Reporter and Autodesk at Sundance that “we need to build a system for ongoing compensation” as the technology depends on “human input.”

He also joined a group of industry insiders last December to form the Creators Coalition on AI, with its mission being to provide “a central coordinating hub to upgrade our industry’s systems and institutions.” The group additionally has an advisory council that seeks “to establish shared standards, definitions and best practices as well as ethical and artistic protections for if and when AI is used in entertainment projects.”

articles.title: Chris Rock Takes a Scalpel to L.A. in ‘Misty Green,’ Makes a Star of Rosalind Eleazar
articles.summary: With its U.S. premiere at the New York Film Festival, the ‘Slow Horses’ actor delivers a stunning lead performance in the comedian’s fourth film as director.
body: Before this starmaking turn, Eleazar built a stateside profile on Apple TV’s Slow Horses alongside Gary Oldman and Kristin Scott Thomas. She spent four seasons on the critics’ darling as Louisa Guy, a disgraced, mourning MI5 agent. Before that, she appeared in the BBC’s Howards End as Jacky Bast, and in between these prestigious TV roles she worked on English stages, having trained at the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art.

That varied résumé was a fitting prelude to Misty Green, a chaotic drama that’s messy, complicated and unapologetic, just like the one-time starlet it follows for a week or so as she moves through Los Angeles watching her life unravel.
